idiom_name: nil interface / zero value placeholder, no-op struct when an implementation is required
implementation_notes: Go's zero values are designed to be usable, so the placeholder is usually nil for interface and pointer parameters and T{} for concrete struct parameters, and the language does not even complain about unused parameters in the callee (only unused local variables are restricted by the spec). Where the SUT demands a non-nil interface, a one-line struct with no-op methods - or a struct whose method fields are empty functions - is the dummy, while blank identifiers name ignored arguments. testify and gomock exist, but they serve queued expectations and interaction assertions, i.e. the stub/mock patterns. The classic Go trap belongs here: an interface holding a typed nil pointer is not nil, so a nil check in the SUT passes and the first method call panics.
code_sketch:
type noopNotifier struct{}

func (noopNotifier) Notify(string) {}      // never called on this path

s := NewSession(cfg, noopNotifier{}, nil /* unused clock */, http.DefaultClient)
s.Run(ctx)                                  // path reads neither clock nor notifier
pitfalls: A nil interface panics only when the SUT calls a method on it, which happens far from the test's setup; if the interface is not provably unused, supply a no-op implementation instead of nil.

An interface holding a typed nil ((*T)(nil)) is non-nil, so a guarded SUT passes the check and then dereferences nil inside the method - the failure looks like a production bug rather than a bad placeholder.
A value-typed no-op struct is copied on every interface conversion; adding recording state to it requires a pointer receiver (and turns it into a spy), so keep dummies stateless.
